So steam engines have existed since as far back as the first century AD, but they were mostly novelties back then. The fuel burns and boils water in the boiler. What we're looking at here is a fire tube boiler, where a series of tubes are run through the main body of the boiler, through which the heat from the firebox flows.

The opposite, a water tube boiler, also exists. It can generate steam much more efficiently, but it was never frequently used in steam locomotives. As the water from the boiler turns to steam, it builds pressure. When the engineer opens the throttle, the steam flows through pipes to the cylinders. The cylinder has four valves on it, two at each end. The steam enters through one valve and expands, moving the piston one way.

Once the steam is expanded, the other valve opens and the steam escapes as steam is forced in from the other side. A device called the valve gear, which is controlled by a reverser lever, alters the timing of these valves, allowing for more efficient use of steam depending on the speed of the train, as well as actually controlling the direction of the locomotive.

How did these railroads get built? Typically, a charter was written up by a state or municipality for a company to build a railroad from one place to another place. These charters typically granted the railroad certain rights, like the right to access private property and survey land, or even delegated powers like eminent domain to the railroad for the purpose of securing right-of-way, or the land the actual tracks sit on.

Right-of-way typically comes in the form of an easement rather than outright land ownership. The railroad doesn't technically own the land, but has nearly all the same rights as a landowner would. Sometimes land grants were offered to the railroad as a means of financing the railroad, especially for those which traveled in very undeveloped territory. The first transcontinental railroad was financed this way. Massive land grants were offered to the railroad as it progressed west.

This land was uninhabited, except of course by the Native Americans who actually lived there, so the government felt entitled to just hand it out to private companies. If not offered land grants, then railroads would typically buy land on each side of their right-of-way as they built. Once the railroad was complete and the trains were running,

The railroad built stations at small towns and crossroads, and the land around them was sold at a huge profit since the railroad made the land more accessible and thus more valuable. This is a pattern which is going to be repeated many times in this series. So especially in the early days, these railroad charters were very vague, stating that a company was to build a road from one place to another place. No one was quite sure how railroads were supposed to work.

Some even provided for the operation of private rail vehicles on the railroad, though this never happened in practice. But the vagueness left them ripe for abuse. If you were clever, you could get a charter to allow you to do something entirely other than what the charter actually stated. with a whole bunch of manual labor. Now, railroads can't travel up steep hills, so the terrain has to be cut and filled where the railroad travels over rough terrain. Most early railroad workers on the East Coast were Irish immigrants, though tunnel work typically called for former miners from Wales and Scotland.

On the west coast, Chinese immigrants were most commonly employed, though railroads on the west coast would not be built for several years. So those were the early railroads. Primitive signaling systems are still decades off, and centralized dispatching wasn't even a dream yet. And air brakes will not arrive until after the Civil War.
